title: Even the urge (Genesis Rabbah 9:7)
hookLine: "very good" includes the urge; without it no one would build a house or marry
tomorrow: the garden was all for Adam. so what was the one catch?

cards: The smell of a rival's new car. A coworker's promotion. The friend whose post blew up while yours sank.
That little burn in the chest doesn't feel holy. Genesis closes its first chapter with God looking at everything: "and, behold, it was very good."
Rabbi Nahman bar Samuel stops on that word very, and makes a claim that sounds almost wrong.

teach.b: In Genesis Rabbah he says: good, that's the good urge.
Very good, that's the yetzer hara, the urge usually called the evil one. Wait: the evil urge is very good? Yes, he answers.
Without it, no one would build a house, marry, have children or open a business.

And he brings Ecclesiastes, where the speaker watches people work and decides that all their labor and skill come from rivalry, one person with another. The yetzer hara here isn't a cartoon devil on your shoulder.
It's drive: wanting, hunger, ambition, the itch to have what they have. Left alone, it wrecks things, which is why it keeps its name. But the midrash refuses to wish it away.
A world without it would be calm and empty: no houses going up, no families, no shop on the corner. The Mishnah has a phrase for the other half: love God with all your heart, with both your urges.
So the claim here is simple and strange. Even the urge belongs to very good.
The fire under the pot can burn the house down.

how: Jewish teaching often speaks of the yetzer hara and the yetzer tov, the two urges; this midrash on Genesis 1:31 is a common text when people study how ambition and desire can serve good ends.

o: a feeling that must be stamped out before prayer
the drive in us, part of what God called very good
a temptation sent from outside to trip people up

games.q: good and very good — tap the pairs.
p: no house, no marriage, no business

s: Judaism teaches that desire itself is evil and should be killed
this midrash calls the urge part of very good: without it, no one builds.
the yetzer hara still keeps the name evil urge
left alone, it wrecks things. the midrash keeps the name and the warning.
the yetzer hara is a devil on your shoulder
here it's drive: wanting, hunger, ambition.

games.q: your little brother asks why he gets so jealous of his friends' stuff, and whether that makes him bad. what does this midrash give you to say?
o: that jealousy is wicked; hope it goes away and never comes back.
that the feeling is a drive; it can wreck things or build things.
that it's fine; whatever you want, you should go and get.
games.why: Rabbi Nahman bar Samuel: very good means the urge too. without it, no one builds a house. it still needs steering.

practice: Make a fist, tight, and feel the heat and pressure build: that's the urge, all push. Hold it for a few breaths.
Then open your hand slowly, palm up, and feel the same strength still there, in fingers that could now carry or build something. Rest in the open hand for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Even the urge: in Genesis Rabbah, very good includes the yetzer hara, the drive without which no one builds a house.

orig.note: Hebrew: the evil urge, the drive this midrash finds inside very good.

carryVoice: For the road: even the urge is good, in steady hands. That's day fifteen seventy-two, done.
